title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
text:
Given a short text description of a business activity — such as “I sell croissants and pains au chocolat” — the goal is to automatically assign the correct NACE 2.1 activity code from hundreds of possible categories. This is a supervised multiclass classification problem.



Two main approaches exist for this task:








Approach
How it works
Best when




Supervised (this notebook)
Train a neural network on labelled examples
Large labelled dataset available, low-latency inference needed


RAG (see notebook 2)
Retrieve similar examples, ask a LLM to decide
Few labelled examples, need for explainability via retrieved context



In this notebook, we use the supervised approach: the model learns directly from thousands of labelled examples and can predict at inference time without calling an external API.








flowchart LR
    A["Labelled data<br/>text + NAF code"] --> B["Split<br/>train / val / test"]
    B --> C["WordPiece Tokenizer<br/>text → token IDs"]
    C --> D["torchTextClassifiers<br/>token IDs → NAF code"]
    D --> E["Evaluation<br/>& explainability"]










How to prepare and split a labelled text dataset
How to train a subword tokenizer (WordPiece) on domain-specific text
How to configure and train a neural text classifier end-to-end
How to load a pretrained model from MLflow and run inference
How to interpret predictions using label attention attributions




Three things need to be in place before running any cell.
1. Install the dependencies
All required packages are listed in pyproject.toml. Run the following command once at the root of the project to install them into a virtual environment:
uv sync
This installs, among others, torchTextClassifiers — the INSEE library that provides the tokenizer, model, and training loop used throughout this notebook. Its full API documentation is available here.
2. Understand what MLflow is and why we need it
In this notebook, we use MLflow in two ways:

During training (Exercise 4), metrics are logged to a remote MLflow server so you can monitor progress.
After training (Exercise 4, Question 3), we download a pretrained model that was already trained on the full dataset and stored in MLflow, so you do not have to wait hours for training to complete.

2. Set up your MLflow credentials
MLflow is an open-source platform for tracking machine learning experiments. Every time a model is trained, MLflow records the hyperparameters used, the metrics obtained (loss, accuracy…), and the model artefacts (weights, tokenizer, configuration). This makes it easy to compare runs, reproduce results, and share trained models with others. This funathon project uses MLflow in multiple ways.
Because the MLflow server is a remote, access-controlled service, you need to provide two pieces of information:

MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI: the URL of the MLflow server (tells your code where to connect).
MLFLOW_RUN_ID: the identifier of the specific training run whose artefacts (pretrained model) you want to download.

These values must not be hardcoded in the notebook — storing credentials in source code is a security risk. Instead, create a file named .env at the root of the project and fill it in as follows:
MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=<add the MLflow server URL>
MLFLOW_RUN_ID=<add the run ID>
The notebook loads this file automatically at startup with load_dotenv(), making the values available as environment variables without ever appearing in the code.

How many unique NAF codes are present in the dataset? This number will define the number of output classes the model must predict.


Clue here

title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
text:
3.1 Question 1 — Split the dataset
Use train_test_split from sklearn.model_selection to split the dataset into train, validation, and test sets (70% / 15% / 15%). Do not forget to choose a random_state.


Clue here

train_test_split splits a dataset in two — call it twice to get three subsets.



Click to see the answer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

train_df, tmp_df = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.30, random_state=42)
val_df, test_df  = train_test_split(tmp_df, test_size=0.50, random_state=42)

X_train = train_df["label"].to_numpy()
X_val   = val_df["label"].to_numpy()
X_test  = test_df["label"].to_numpy()

print(f"Train: {len(train_df)} | Val: {len(val_df)} | Test: {len(test_df)}")


Use LabelEncoder from sklearn.preprocessing (see here for the documentation). Call .fit() on all codes, then .transform() on each split. Extract numpy arrays with .to_numpy().






NoteWhy do we use LabelEncoder ?





We use LabelEncoder to map the categorical target y to integers 0, 1, …, n_classes - 1, the format expected by scikit-learn classifiers. It should not be used on input features, however: for those, OrdinalEncoder or OneHotEncoder is preferred, because LabelEncoder is designed for a 1D target and does not handle unseen categories at inference time.



The code column contains strings like "47.11A". Neural networks do not understand strings and require integer targets (1, 2, 3…), so we need to map each unique NAF code to an integer index. Encode the code column of each split using LabelEncoder from sklearn.preprocessing, and keep the fitted encoder — you will need it later to convert integer predictions back to NAF code strings.






WarningWatch out for unseen categories!





Always fit the LabelEncoder on all codes present in the data, not just codes present in the training set. Why that? Imagine that one code is very rare and is present only in the validation set or in the test. If the LabelEncoder is trained on the training set alone, it will not be able to map this rare code to an integer, and when you apply the LabelEncoder to this code (for instance when evaluating the model) you will get an error.





Click to see the answer
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

encoder = LabelEncoder()
encoder.fit(df['code'].to_numpy())

y_train = encoder.transform(train_df['code'].to_numpy())
y_val   = encoder.transform(val_df['code'].to_numpy())
y_test  = encoder.transform(test_df['code'].to_numpy())

title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
text:
4.1 Why tokenization?
Neural networks can only work with numbers because they have no notion of letters or words. A tokenizer is the component that bridges this gap: it converts raw text into a sequence of integers that the model can process.
The process has three steps:

Split the text into small units called tokens: these can be whole words, subword fragments, or individual characters.
Map each token to a unique integer using a fixed vocabulary (a lookup table built during training).
Pad or truncate the resulting sequence to a fixed length so that all inputs have the same shape, which is required for batched training.

The diagram below illustrates this pipeline on a short example:
flowchart LR
    A["\"I sell croissants\""] -->|"split into tokens"| B["[\"i\", \"sell\", \"croi\", \"##ssants\"]"]
    B -->|"look up in vocabulary"| C["[45, 112, 87, 203]"]
    C -->|"pad to length 6"| D["[45, 112, 87, 203, 0, 0]"]

title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
text:
4.2 Why subword tokenization?
There are several ways to split text into tokens: by character, by full word, or by subword fragment. Each has trade-offs:








Strategy
Example for “croissants”
Problem




Character-level
["c","r","o","i","s","s","a","n","t","s"]
Sequences become very long; meaning is hard to capture


Word-level
["croissants"]
Rare or misspelled words get mapped to [UNKNOWN]


Subword (WordPiece)
["croi", "##ssants"]
Handles rare words without losing common subparts



WordPiece, the algorithm used here, builds a vocabulary of frequent subword units from the training corpus. Words it has never seen can still be represented by combining known fragments. The ## prefix marks a fragment that continues the previous token (i.e. it is not the start of a new word).
Because the vocabulary is learned from your data, it naturally adapts to domain-specific vocabulary; in our case, French business descriptions full of technical terms.






NoteWant to go further?






The Hugging Face tokenizer documentation gives a clear overview of the main tokenization strategies (BPE, WordPiece, Unigram).
The Hugging Face tokenizers course chapter is a hands-on introduction for beginners.










Tip Exercice 3: Train a WordPiece tokenizer





4.3 Question 1 — Train the tokenizer and inspect a sample
Train a WordPieceTokenizer from scratch on the training labels with vocab_size=5000 and output_dim=125. Inspect a sample tokenization to understand how the text is split.
Instantiate WordPieceTokenizer(vocab_size=5000, output_dim=125) and call .train(X_train). Use .tokenize() and .convert_ids_to_tokens() to inspect a sample.






WarningTokenizer data leakage





Always train the tokenizer on X_train only — never on the validation or test set. Using the full dataset would mean the tokenizer has seen vocabulary from examples the model is supposed to predict blind.





Click to see the answer
from torchTextClassifiers.tokenizers import WordPieceTokenizer

tokenizer = WordPieceTokenizer(vocab_size=5000, output_dim=125)
tokenizer.train(X_train)

print("Output tensor size:", tokenizer.tokenize(X_train[0]).input_ids.shape)
print("Tokens:", tokenizer.tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(
    tokenizer.tokenize(X_train[0]).input_ids.squeeze(0)
))
print("Vocabulary size:", tokenizer.vocab_size)

title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
text:
6.1 Question 1 — Instantiate the classifier
Instantiate the classifier from a ModelConfig and the trained tokenizer.
Build an AttentionConfig, then a ModelConfig with embedding_dim, num_classes, and a LabelAttentionConfig. Pass both to torchTextClassifiers(tokenizer=..., model_config=...).






NoteKey parameters






embedding_dim=96: size of the dense vector representing each token. Larger values capture more information but are slower to train.
n_layers=1, n_head=4: the self-attention has 1 transformer layer with 4 parallel attention heads. More heads can capture richer patterns but increase computation.
sequence_len=tokenizer.output_dim: must match the tokenizer’s output_dim so that all token sequences have the same length.






Click to see the answer
from torchTextClassifiers import ModelConfig, TrainingConfig, torchTextClassifiers
from torchTextClassifiers.model.components import AttentionConfig
from torchTextClassifiers.model.components.text_embedder import LabelAttentionConfig

attention_config = AttentionConfig(
    n_layers=1, n_head=4, n_kv_head=4,
    sequence_len=tokenizer.output_dim,
)

embedding_dim = 96

model_config = ModelConfig(
    embedding_dim=embedding_dim,
    num_classes=n_classes,
    attention_config=attention_config,
    label_attention_config=LabelAttentionConfig(n_head=4, num_classes=n_classes),
)

ttc = torchTextClassifiers(tokenizer=tokenizer, model_config=model_config)

title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
section: 6.2 Question 2 — Train on a small subsample
text:
6.2 Question 2 — Train on a small subsample
Define a TrainingConfig and train on a small subsample so it completes quickly.
Create a TrainingConfig(lr=..., batch_size=..., num_epochs=..., num_workers=...) and call ttc.train(X_train=..., y_train=..., X_val=..., y_val=..., training_config=..., verbose=True).
You can see the TrainingConfig documentation here






NoteNote





We train on a small subsample (5% of the data, 1 epoch) just to verify the pipeline runs end-to-end — the model will not converge to a good accuracy in one epoch on 5% of the data. A model trained on the full dataset for many epochs is loaded from MLflow in the next step.
Key hyperparameters used here:

lr=1e-3: a standard starting learning rate for Adam-based optimizers.
batch_size=256: how many examples are processed before each weight update — larger batches are faster but require more memory.
num_epochs=1: one pass over the data, kept short for this demo.
num_workers=0: disables parallel data loading (use >0 to speed up on multi-core machines).






Click to see the answer
TRAIN_FRAC = 0.05
VAL_FRAC = 0.05

X_train_small = X_train[:int(len(X_train) * TRAIN_FRAC)]
y_train_small = y_train[:int(len(y_train) * TRAIN_FRAC)]
X_val_small   = X_val[:int(len(X_val) * VAL_FRAC)]
y_val_small   = y_val[:int(len(y_val) * VAL_FRAC)]

training_config = TrainingConfig(
    lr=1e-3,
    batch_size=256,
    num_epochs=1,
    num_workers=0,
)

ttc.train(
    X_train=X_train_small,
    y_train=y_train_small,
    X_val=X_val_small,
    y_val=y_val_small,
    training_config=training_config,
    verbose=True,
)

title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
section: 6.3 Question 3 — Load the pretrained model from MLflow
text:
6.3 Question 3 — Load the pretrained model from MLflow
Load the pretrained model trained on the full dataset from MLflow.
You can see the documentation on MLFlow Python API here
Use mlflow.set_tracking_uri() then mlflow.artifacts.download_artifacts(f"runs:/{RUN_ID}/model_artifacts"). Rebuild the model from model_config.json and restore weights with load_state_dict().


Clue here

mlflow.artifacts.download_artifacts fetches all saved files locally. We rebuild the model architecture from model_config.json and restore the weights with load_state_dict.







NoteNote





Set MLFLOW_RUN_ID in your .env file to the right run ID.





Click to see the answer
import mlflow
import json
import torch
from transformers import PreTrainedTokenizerFast

MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI = os.environ["MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI"]
RUN_ID = os.environ["MLFLOW_RUN_ID"]

mlflow.set_tracking_uri(MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI)

artifacts_path = mlflow.artifacts.download_artifacts(f"runs:/{RUN_ID}/model_artifacts")

with open(os.path.join(artifacts_path, "model_config.json")) as f:
    saved_config = json.load(f)

with open(os.path.join(artifacts_path, "label_mapping.json")) as f:
    saved_label_mapping = json.load(f)  # {str(int): NAF code}

loaded_tokenizer = WordPieceTokenizer(
    vocab_size=saved_config["vocab_size"],
    output_dim=saved_config["output_dim"],
)
loaded_tokenizer.tokenizer = PreTrainedTokenizerFast.from_pretrained(
    os.path.join(artifacts_path, "tokenizer")
)
loaded_tokenizer.trained = True

loaded_model_config = ModelConfig(
    embedding_dim=saved_config["embedding_dim"],
    num_classes=saved_config["num_classes"],
    attention_config=AttentionConfig(
        n_layers=saved_config["n_layers"],
        n_head=saved_config["n_head"],
        n_kv_head=saved_config["n_kv_head"],
        sequence_len=saved_config["output_dim"],
    ),
    label_attention_config=LabelAttentionConfig(
        n_head=saved_config["label_attention_n_head"],
        num_classes=saved_config["num_classes"],
    ),
)

ttc_full = torchTextClassifiers(tokenizer=loaded_tokenizer, model_config=loaded_model_config)
ttc_full.pytorch_model.load_state_dict(
    torch.load(os.path.join(artifacts_path, "model_state_dict.pt"), weights_only=True)
)
ttc_full.pytorch_model.eval()

title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
section: 7.1 Question 1 — Generate top-3 predictions with confidence scores
text:
7.1 Question 1 — Generate top-3 predictions with confidence scores
Call ttc_full.predict(np.array(example_texts), top_k=3, explain_with_label_attention=True). The result is a dict with keys prediction and confidence — decode integer predictions back to NAF codes using saved_label_mapping[str(idx)].


Click to see the answer
import numpy as np

top_k = 3

example_texts = [
    "I sell croissants and pains au chocolat in my bakery",
    "I develop business management software for companies",
    "I repair cars and carry out technical inspections",
]

results = ttc_full.predict(np.array(example_texts), top_k=top_k, explain_with_label_attention=True)

for i, text in enumerate(example_texts):
    predicted_codes = [saved_label_mapping[str(results["prediction"][i][k].item())] for k in range(top_k)]
    confidence = [results["confidence"][i][k].item() for k in range(top_k)]
    print(f"\nText: {text}")
    for code, conf in zip(predicted_codes, confidence):
        print(f"  {code}  (confidence: {conf:.3f})")

title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
section: 7.2 Question 2 — Visualise word attributions for the top prediction
text:
7.2 Question 2 — Visualise word attributions for the top prediction
Extract label_attention_attributions from the results, average over attention heads, then use map_attributions_to_word(), map_attributions_to_char(), plot_attributions_at_word(), and plot_attributions_at_char() from torchTextClassifiers.utilities.plot_explainability.






NoteUnderstanding the result fields






label_attention_attributions: tensor of shape (n_head, num_classes, seq_len) — the attention score each class gave to each token, across all heads.
offset_mapping: character-level start/end positions of each token in the original string, used to map token-level scores back to characters.
word_ids: maps each token to its parent word index, used to aggregate token scores at the word level.






Click to see the answer
from torchTextClassifiers.utilities.plot_explainability import (
    map_attributions_to_char, map_attributions_to_word,
    plot_attributions_at_char, plot_attributions_at_word, figshow,
)

text_idx = 0
top_k_idx = 0
text_sample         = example_texts[text_idx]
offsets             = results["offset_mapping"][text_idx]
word_ids            = results["word_ids"][text_idx]
predicted_class_idx = results["prediction"][text_idx][top_k_idx].item()
predicted_code      = saved_label_mapping[str(predicted_class_idx)]

# Average attention over heads, pick the row for the predicted class
attn_matrix  = results["label_attention_attributions"][text_idx].detach()  # (n_head, num_classes, seq_len)
attributions = attn_matrix.mean(dim=0)[predicted_class_idx]                # (seq_len,)

words, word_attributions = map_attributions_to_word(
    attributions.unsqueeze(0), text_sample, word_ids, offsets
)
char_attributions = map_attributions_to_char(attributions.unsqueeze(0), offsets, text_sample)

titles = [f"Attributions for NAF code {predicted_code}"]

figshow(plot_attributions_at_char(
    text=text_sample, attributions_per_char=char_attributions, titles=titles,
)[0])

figshow(plot_attributions_at_word(
    text=text_sample, words=words.values(), attributions_per_word=word_attributions, titles=titles,
)[0])

title: Supervised approach using TorchTextClassifiers
section: 7.3 Question 3 — Evaluate accuracy on the test set
text:
7.3 Question 3 — Evaluate accuracy on the test set
Run ttc_full.predict(X_test_small, top_k=1) and compare the predictions against y_test_small to compute accuracy.


Click to see the answer
TEST_FRAC = 0.05
X_test_small = X_test[:int(len(X_test) * TEST_FRAC)]
y_test_small = y_test[:int(len(y_test) * TEST_FRAC)]

results_test = ttc_full.predict(X_test_small, top_k=1)

preds    = results_test["prediction"].squeeze(1).numpy()
accuracy = (preds == y_test_small).mean()
print(f"Test accuracy: {accuracy:.4f} ({int(accuracy * len(y_test_small))}/{len(y_test_small)} correct)")




Clue here

predict() returns a dictionary with prediction (shape (N, top_k)) and confidence (shape (N, top_k)). Use saved_label_mapping[str(idx)] to decode integer predictions back to NAF code strings. Words highlighted in red contributed positively to the prediction; those in blue pulled the model away from it.
